blocks.text: Design a general-purpose messaging queue, the kind of system behind Kafka or a similar log-based broker, that lets producers publish messages and lets multiple, entirely independent downstream systems each consume the same stream at their own pace. This is a genuinely different model from a traditional, destructive-read queue, where reading a message removes it, one consumer's progress here must never affect another's, and a message needs to remain available for replay long after it was first read, not vanish the instant any single consumer processes it.

blocks.alt: A published message is appended to its partition's durable, retained log, and multiple independent consumer groups can each read it at their own pace without affecting each other

blocks.text: The technique that makes this possible is a partitioned, append-only log combined with per-consumer-group offset tracking, the broker retains every message for a configured period regardless of who has read it, and each consumer group independently remembers its own position in that log, letting entirely separate systems consume the exact same stream without any coordination between them.

blocks.text: A producer should be able to publish a message to a topic, optionally with a key determining which partition it lands in. A consumer group should be able to read messages from a topic starting from its own last committed position. Multiple, independent consumer groups should be able to consume the exact same topic at their own pace without interfering with each other. Messages within a single partition should be delivered in the exact order they were published.

blocks.alt: Strict ordering within a partition, multiple independent consumers of the same stream, durable and replayable message retention, horizontally scalable throughput, and per-topic access control

blocks.text: Strict ordering within a partition means messages sharing the same key must be processed in the exact order they were originally published. Multiple independent consumers of the same stream means two entirely different downstream systems, say an analytics pipeline and a notification service, should each be able to read the same published messages at their own pace, on their own schedule. Durable, replayable retention means a message should still exist to be read again long after it was first consumed, not disappear the instant one reader happens to process it. Horizontally scalable throughput means total capacity grows by adding more partitions and more consumers, not by making one giant, single-threaded stream faster. And per-topic access control means only authorized producers and consumers should be able to write to, or read from, a given topic at all.

blocks.text: This design assumes at-least-once delivery, a consumer commits its offset only after successfully processing a batch, so a crash before committing safely re-reads the same messages rather than ever silently skipping them; exactly-once semantics are treated as an idempotent-consumer concern layered on top, not something the broker itself guarantees. Partitioning by message key is assumed the default, guaranteeing per-key ordering while still allowing overall parallelism across many partitions. Retention is assumed to be a configurable time window, independent of whether any particular consumer group has actually read a given message yet.

class MessageQueue:
    # A partitioned, append-only, retained message log with independent
    # per-consumer-group offset tracking, the core Kafka-style pub/sub model:
    # reading a message never removes it, and different groups can be at
    # completely different positions in the same log at the same time.
    def __init__(self):
        self.partitions = {}       # partitionId -> retained, ordered messages
        self.offsets_by_group = {}  # groupId -> {partitionId: next offset to read}

    def publish(self, partition_id, payload):
        self.partitions.setdefault(partition_id, []).append(payload)  # appended, never removed on read

    def poll(self, group_id, partition_id, max_messages):
        log = self.partitions.get(partition_id, [])
        group_offsets = self.offsets_by_group.setdefault(group_id, {})
        current_offset = group_offsets.get(partition_id, 0)  # this group's own position, independent of any other group

        end = min(len(log), current_offset + max_messages)
        result = log[current_offset:end]

        group_offsets[partition_id] = end  # advance only this group's own offset
        return result

    def partition_size(self, partition_id):
        return len(self.partitions.get(partition_id, []))


def main():
    queue = MessageQueue()

    # A producer publishes 3 messages to partition 0.
    queue.publish(0, "order-created")
    queue.publish(0, "order-paid")
    queue.publish(0, "order-shipped")

    # Consumer group "analytics" polls and reads all 3 messages, advancing its own offset to 3.
    print("analytics poll 1:", queue.poll("analytics", 0, 10))

    # Consumer group "notifications" is entirely independent: it has never read partition 0 before,
    # so it also starts from offset 0 and reads the exact same 3 messages, unaffected by "analytics".
    print("notifications poll 1:", queue.poll("notifications", 0, 10))

    # A 4th message is published.
    queue.publish(0, "order-delivered")

    # "analytics" only gets the new message, since its own offset was already at 3.
    print("analytics poll 2 (only new messages):", queue.poll("analytics", 0, 10))

    # "notifications" also only gets the new message, since its own offset was independently at 3 too.
    print("notifications poll 2 (only new messages):", queue.poll("notifications", 0, 10))

    # The log itself still holds all 4 messages, retained regardless of either group's consumption.
    print("Partition 0 still retains all published messages:", queue.partition_size(0))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items: Architecture: a partitioned, durable, retained message log read independently by multiple consumer groups, each tracking its own offset, with partition ownership rebalanced within a group as membership changes.
Capacity: millions of messages per second across many partitions, several independent consumer groups reading the same topic, and hours-to-days retention enabling replay.
The core techniques: a partitioned append-only log and independent per-consumer-group offset tracking, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: partition logs distributed across broker nodes, alongside a small, frequently-updated, group-and-partition-keyed offset store.
End-to-end workflows: a publish-and-independent-consume flow and a consumer rebalance flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: strict ordering guaranteed within a partition, with no ordering guarantee at all across different partitions.

Trade-offs: a partitioned retained log versus a traditional destructive-read queue versus synchronous broadcast with no persistence, compared directly on support for multiple independent consumers and message retention.
